summary: Defines a small set of X.509v3 certificates and keys for use when producing sample S/MIME signed or encrypted messages. Having shared example material makes it easier for the S/MIME community to exchange samples and test interoperability. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of practice keys that everyone can use to try out secure email without risking real ones.

subtitle: Shared example keys and certificates for testing secure email implementations.

tldr.problem: S/MIME developers need a common set of test certificates and keys to share samples of signed and encrypted messages for interoperability testing and development, but existing examples are outdated and use weak cryptography.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a new set of X.509v3 certificates and their corresponding private keys, including both RSA and Ed25519 certification authorities with sample end-entity certificates for four fictional personas, along with password-protected PKCS #12 objects for deployment testing.
tldr.outcome: Developers can exchange S/MIME test messages with known keys, making it easier to test implementations for correctness and interoperability without needing to generate their own test infrastructure.

today: RFC 9216 is an Informational RFC that provides test certificates and keys for S/MIME development and interoperability testing. These materials remain the current standard for developers who need to exchange test messages and validate their implementations.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The S/MIME community needs shared, publicly available certificates and keys for testing. Without them, developers cannot easily create test samples of signed or encrypted messages that others can verify and process. This document provides a standard set of test certificates that any implementer can use.

The RFC provides an RSA Certification Authority with two sample end-entity certificates (for Alice and Bob), and an Ed25519 Certification Authority with two more sample certificates (for Carlos and Dana). Each certificate comes with its corresponding private key, making it possible to create test messages that have valid signatures or decryption.

Unlike earlier test materials, these certificates use modern cryptography: 2048-bit RSA and Ed25519 signatures. All certificates are marked as test-only with certificate policies, preventing accidental use in production systems.
sections.plainLanguage: To test email encryption, everyone needs to agree on some practice locks. This document gives everyone the same practice locks so they can all test together.

sections.title: Design and Usage Considerations
sections.content:
All certificates in this document are self-signed or cross-signed by test CAs, not by any real trusted root. A tool using these certificates must explicitly trust the example CAs provided. The certificates expire in 2052, far enough in the future to remain useful for many years.

The certificate chains can be used in two ways: either as a two-certificate chain (end-entity signed directly by root CA) or as a three-certificate chain (with an intermediate CA). The document provides both an RSA root CA and an Ed25519 root CA, plus a cross-signed RSA-to-Ed25519 intermediate certificate, allowing flexible testing scenarios.

The certificates carry no revocation information. They do not include OCSP responders or CRL distribution points because test suites are expected to run offline. This makes them unsuitable for testing revocation handling, but appropriate for basic signature and encryption testing.

All private keys are provided in two formats: as PEM-encoded PKCS #8 (unencrypted) and as PKCS #12 objects (password-protected). This allows testing of both password-less and password-protected key material.
sections.plainLanguage: These practice locks are specifically marked as for testing only. They include an expiration date far in the future. Tools have to manually say they trust these practice locks.

sections.title: Certification Authorities and Keys
sections.content:
The document provides two certification authorities. The RSA CA uses a 2048-bit RSA key and signs certificates using SHA-256. The Ed25519 CA uses the Ed25519 signature algorithm, a modern elliptic curve approach that is faster and smaller than RSA.

All RSA keys are derived deterministically using the Provable Prime Generation method specified in FIPS 186-4, based on SHA-256 hashes of seed strings. This allows anyone to recreate the keys using the documented seeds. The seeds and derivation parameters are stored in the private key objects themselves.

The Ed25519 keys are derived by hashing simple strings. The document includes the seeds and derivation methods so that implementations with appropriate tooling can recreate them if needed.

The RSA CA provides a cross-signed certificate: its certificate is signed by the Ed25519 CA. This enables a testing scenario where a client only trusts the Ed25519 root but can still validate RSA end-entity certificates through the intermediate.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two practice CAs: one using RSA (older, larger) and one using Ed25519 (newer, smaller). Each can sign certificates. Their keys are made in a way that anyone can recreate them from a seed number.

sections.title: End-Entity Certificates and Use Cases
sections.content:
Four fictional personas have certificates: Alice Lovelace (alice@smime.example), Bob Smith (bob@smime.example), Carlos Santiago, and Dana Johnson. Each has two certificates: one marked for signature verification (signing) and one marked for encryption (key encipherment).

This separation of signing and encryption keys allows testing of implementations that handle key purpose restrictions. A signature key can be used to create or verify digital signatures. An encryption key can be used to encrypt data or decrypt received data. Many S/MIME implementations require these to be separate.

Each certificate includes the corresponding end-entity private key in PKCS #8 format. Additionally, the document provides PKCS #12 objects (password-protected containers) for each persona, bundling the signing and encryption keys together. The passwords for these objects are simple strings, allowing implementations to test password-based key import.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice, Bob, Carlos, and Dana each get two practice keys: one for signing things and one for hiding secrets. Developers can use these to test sending signed or secret emails.

sections.title: Testing and Security
sections.content:
These certificates are explicitly marked as test-only and should never be used for real communication. Each carries certificate policies (OID 2.16.840.1.101.3.2.1.48.1) indicating they are for testing only. Any proper implementation should reject these when configured for production use.

The passwords for PKCS #12 objects are documented and simple. These objects are for testing password-protected key import, not for secure storage. Implementation developers should test their password-handling code with these examples.

The document notes that these certificates are unsuitable for testing certificate expiration handling (because they expire far in the future) or revocation testing (because they include no revocation information). Separate test data would be needed for those scenarios.

The seeds and generation parameters for all keys are public, so anyone can recreate them. These keys have no secrets—they are entirely unsuitable for real use. Only implementations that explicitly know these are test keys should trust certificates signed by these CAs.
sections.plainLanguage: These practice locks are clearly marked as fake. Their passwords are published. Anyone can create new ones using the recipe. They should never be used for real secrets.
